title: Bluebell and the Best Berries
markdown:
The sun stretched golden fingers over Willow Creek. Each blade of grass wore a bead of dew. Sunny Meadow smelled of warm earth, opening blossoms, and bees already at their humming. Bluebell the bunny twitched her nose. Whiskers trembled. Today was strawberry-picking day.

By the old wooden garden gate, Mr. Sprig the snail polished his shell with a bit of damp moss until the browns and creams shone like a small galaxy. He loved strawberries whole and round, not sad squished puddles.

“Good morning, Bluebell,” he called, a soft stretched hum.

“Good morning, Mr. Sprig.” Her white tail bounced. “Ready to see who can bring the juiciest strawberries home the fastest?”

He smiled, slow, eyes crinkling. “I am ready. But the fastest way is not always the best way, when the fruit is so precious. Rushing through tickly grass sounds rather energetic for delicate berries.”

Bluebell giggled, bells in the sound. She already had a plan. The juiciest strawberries, the ones that tasted of sunshine, grew at the back of Farmer McGregor’s patch. She knew a shortcut that wiggled through the tallest tickliest grass. It would save so much hopping.

“You can take the sensible path. I’ll see you at the finish, way before you.”

A flash of white, and she was a streak in the green sea. Mr. Sprig watched, a knowing twinkle, then set off along the winding path. Antennae swayed like curious flags.

Bluebell hopped and tumbled. Grass tickled her nose and brushed her ears. A seed stuck to a whisker; she left it there, a badge of speed. Sun on her back like a blanket. Paws thudded on cool earth. Once she thought she saw the garden gate already, but it was only a pale stone. She laughed at herself and hopped harder. A splendid shortcut. She could almost taste rubies waiting in her paws. She picked in a happy rush: the first berry, the second, a third that stained her chin, all tumbled into her basket as if the basket were a finish line.

Mr. Sprig took the long way in his own quiet. Sunlight played peek-a-boo through the oak. A robin chattered about a nest, then about a worm, then about the nest again. He paused for a ladybug with seven perfect spots and counted them twice, because counting is a kind of politeness. The path was longer, smooth as a calm stream. When he reached Farmer McGregor’s patch he did not dive. He tasted the air, chose the biggest reddest berries, picked each with a delicate mouth, and set it in his woven leaf basket as if placing a sleeping bee. They sat plump and undisturbed. A late bee inspected his work and, finding no argument, left.

Bluebell burst from the grass at her burrow, basket overflowing, bright and beautiful. A seed still rode her whisker. “I’m home.” She set the basket down with a thump that was meant to be a fanfare. Pride lasted until she looked down. The strawberries at the bottom, picked first and bumped most, were bruised. Juice made a sticky puddle that found a hole in the weave. They looked sad and smushed, more jam than jewel. A little sigh. Crushed clover and damp earth rose around her. She thought of Mr. Sprig’s flags of antennae, still somewhere on the long path, and of how loud her own hop had been.

Mr. Sprig arrived then, shell gleaming, basket upright. Every berry round, red, whole. Bluebell’s tummy rumbled with a quieter wish.

He looked at her basket, then at her droopy ears. He did not say he had told her so. He nudged his basket closer. “Would you like to share? They are quite delicious, if I do say so.”

“My strawberries are all messy,” she whispered.

He offered one perfect berry, rolling it as if it might bruise from a harsh word. She took it. Still warm. Sweet as a good idea. She looked at the ladybug he had admired, now climbing a stem as if the afternoon were a ladder, and at the little basket that had kept its jewels safe. The quick grass had made her fruit sad. His careful path had kept his fruit itself. She tasted again, slower, and the sweetness stayed long enough to be noticed, like a tune you only hear when you stop hopping.

They sat by the burrow and shared. First his berry, then, if she asked, another. Birds sang the ordinary afternoon. A fluffy cloud drifted, in no hurry at all. Bluebell lined her remaining whole berries in a careful row, the way Mr. Sprig’s basket had taught her without speaking. The smushed ones she set aside for jam, if jam is what you call a sweet mess eaten with a friend. She did not announce a moral. She only licked juice from a paw, watched Mr. Sprig’s antennae sway, and let the next strawberry wait until she was ready, which, for once, was not the fastest moment in the meadow.
